title: 1,700-Year-Old Fragment of Homer's 'Odyssey' Discovered in Dutch Archive
snippet: A researcher examining ancient manuscripts in the Netherlands unearthed a rare 4th-century pocket-sized fragment of Homer's epic poem.
content:
While combing through a collection of ancient Egyptian manuscripts at a library in the Netherlands, a researcher made an extraordinary discovery tucked away among the archives: a tiny, 1,700-year-old parchment fragment containing lines from Homer’s epic masterpiece, the "Odyssey."

Mark de Kreij, a professor of Greek literature at Radboud University, came across the miniature piece of history while analyzing early Christian texts at the Utrecht University library. Measuring just 2.6 by 3 inches, the parchment features verses from Book 12 of the epic, detailing the pivotal moment when Odysseus' crew slaughters the sacred cattle of the sun god Helios—an act of sacrilege that leads to the total destruction of their ship and crew.

A Rare Ancient Pocket Edition

"There are so many boring parts in the Odyssey," de Kreij remarked in an interview with Dutch news outlet RTV Utrecht. "This happens to be a really fun passage."

Experts believe the fragment originated as part of a pocket-sized codex produced in Egypt’s Fayum oasis around A.D. 300. Designed for easy travel, the compact booklet was essentially an ancient precursor to modern paperbacks. According to researchers, only about 30 similar fragments from this era have ever been recovered. De Kreij suggested the passage likely survived over a millennium because its position near the middle of the original codex offered it extra protection from the elements.

A Banner Year for Homeric Discoveries

The find marks the second time this year that a lost fragment of Homeric literature has unexpectedly surfaced. Last spring, archaeologists working in Egypt uncovered papyrus fragments of the "Iliad" preserved inside a Roman-era mummy.

Both the "Iliad" and the "Odyssey" were composed in the late eighth or early seventh century B.C. and remain foundational texts of Western literature. How this specific piece ended up in Utrecht's Egyptian collection remains a mystery, but de Kreij will share his full research on the text in an upcoming book examining the university's Greco-Roman manuscripts.
